subtopic: SATELLITE STATES OF EASTERN EUROPE

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: SATELLITE STATES OF EASTERN EUROPE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like at this time to answer the question asked me yesterday by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) about religious persecutions in eastern Europe.
During the past few weeks, Mr. Speaker, this house and the country as a whole have watched with deepening concern what appears to be a systematic campaign of religious persecution in all the satellite states of eastern Europe, but particularly in Hungary where within a short space of time the heads of three branches of the Christian church, the Roman Catholic, the Calvinist and the Lutheran, have either been sentenced to severe punishment or driven into exile. More recent persecutions in Bulgaria seem to be following the same pattern.
The government of Canada has already indicated in the most positive terms and in language clear beyond all possibility of mistake, its abhorrence of this systematic persecution. In a statement on New Year's day I said that the increasingly brutal persecutions of religious. leaders in countries behind the iron curtain have shocked all civilized people. These views were reiterated and strengthened on February 2 by the Secretary of State for External Affairs. In the light of more recent developments, I now wish to reaffirm the position of the Canadian government.
Immediately after the arrest of Cardinal Mindszenty, Primate of Hungary, the Canadian government, as a signatory of the peace treaty, asked our diplomatic representatives
in a number of European capitals and Washington to secure all the available information and to report any steps that might be anticipated on the part of the governments to which they were accredited. Careful study was given also to official intelligence from other sources and to press reports.
This was followed, as the house will recall from the statement made on February 2 by the Secretary of the State of External Affairs, by a communication to the Hungarian government, through the Hungarian minister in Washington, protesting strongly against a policy of repression and religious persecution which appeared to destroy religious freedom in Hungary and appeared also to violate obligations to secure the enjoyment of human rights, including freedom of religious worship, to which Hungary was pledged under the treaty of peace of 1947.
In this message, particular reference was made to the arrest not only of Cardinal Mindszenty, but also of the senior bishop of the Lutheran church in Hungary, and to the flight into exile, under force of persecution, of the senior bishop of the Calvinist church in Hungary.
It seems clear from these incidents that all religious faiths were involved and that a general attack was being launched on the fundamental freedoms of human society. Fresh emphasis was given to the repressive character of these arrests by the conditions under which the trial of Cardinal Mindszenty was conducted. It can hardly be said that these proceedings bear any resemblance to what we understand by a "fair trial". From official sources in which we have confidence, we learn, for example, the following facts about the conduct of this case.
The trial which involved seven persons and four different charges, including capital charges, was concluded in three days. No witnesses were called for the defence. The counsel for the prosecution made no attempt to establish his case but confined himself for the most part to enlarging on the political fairness of the trial. The counsel for the defence put no case for the defence and did not contest easily refutable statements made by the counsel for the prosecution; and the material evidence consisted of statements taken outside the court before the trial. It may be added that no representatives of non-communist governments were permitted

Religious Persecution
to attend the trial. We are informed also that the representative of the government of Australia attempted to visit Budapest for this purpose, but though a visa was promised op six occasions, it was not forthcoming.
Meanwhile the government is continuing to seek the views of like-minded governments, signatory to the treaty, on the character and desirability of any further action that may be taken jointly or independently. It has been suggested, for example, that the treaty of peace be invoked. Unfortunately, the procedures which are immediately available under the treaty of peace all depend for their effectiveness on the co-operation of the soviet government. Since the U.S.S.R. not only supports but even encourages governments which it can influence in their hostility to religion, it is not likely to give the other signatories to the peace treaties much assistance in putting a halt to religious persecution in eastern Europe. It may be, however, that the signatories to the treaties, even without the support of the soviet union, could, through joint representation based on these provisions of these treaties, have some influence upon the governments which are responsible for these acts.
Provision is also made in the treaty for a procedure leading to the establishment of a commission of three to act in regard to any dispute arising out of the execution or interpretation of the treaty. The majority decision, of this commission would be binding on the parties to the dispute.
If this procedure were used, the obstruction of the U.S.S.R. to action under it could not become effective until efforts were made to give effect to the decisions of the commission.
A further possibility that has received some public notice is that the matter be referred to the United Nations; because it would seem obvious that the spirit of repression and persecution that pervades the events under review is clearly not in keeping with the charter of the United Nations or the declaration of human rights.
In any case it is the view of the government that a state which fails to carry out its treaty obligations in letter and spirit cannot expect to be supported in its application for admission to the United Nations; and indeed might expect formally to be condemned by the world organization.
But, Mr. Speaker, in examining these or any other suggestions that may be made, the government's course will be guided by considerations that are more significant than tactics or gestures. While giving the fullest expression to our profound abhorrence of religious persecution, however it may be disguised, we shall seek to take only such action

as appears to offer a reasonable prospect of promoting the principles in which we believe and at the same time of ameliorating the situation with which we are faced in the communist countries.
The events in Hungary have, as hon. members know, been followed by similar action on the part of the Bulgarian government. On February 10 that government issued its indictment of fifteen Protestant leaders in that country, charging them with espionage and other crimes.
The government has instructed the Canadian charge d'affaires in Prague to apply for visas to visit Hungary and Roumania in order that he may make inquiries on the spot and report to the government. Canada is not a signatory to the Bulgarian treaty, but, in any joint action that may be considered advisable, this country would find no difficulty in associating itself with such action. The principles of religious freedom and fundamental human rights are not confined to the articles of a peace treaty.
The clear and common sense conclusion, Mr. Speaker, is that the cases of each church, each bishop, or each group of religious leaders, are horrifying incidents in what appears to be a grand design, a calculated policy of persecution, aimed not perhaps at the immediate extermination of the Christian communions, but at their ultimate subjugation and servitude. By its nature and its dogma, Marxist communism must secure the total obedience of its subjects and cannot tolerate the free speculations of the human spirit and conscience.
A plain recital of a few only of the incidents in this process reveals the pattern of persecution which is swiftly being drawn over the unhappy Christians of these lands. We are already familiar with the fate in Hungary of leaders of three different churches; and I have mentioned the indictments on February 10 by the Bulgarian government of fifteen Protestant leaders in that country. It is noteworthy that while these clergymen, all members of the United Evangelical church in Bulgaria, were apparently arrested some months ago, no indictment was made until this late date.
In Poland some twenty-six priests have been detained and eight arrested for having read a pastoral letter from their bishop in which the anti-religious actions of government officials were severely criticized.
In Czechoslovakia towards the end of last year two members of the Greek Catholic church were tried for alleged espionage activities, and early this month a new campaign was started against the church.
In Roumania in December, 1948, the Roumanian Uniate church, a branch of the Roman Catholic church, was practically extinguished

by government decree and its property confiscated.
It cannot be expected, I am sorry to say, that the tale is ended. From the Baltic to the frontiers of Greece the ceaseless pressure to impose a total communist pattern goes forward. The middle way of life, the only way broad enough to contain in peace and tolerance all creeds and all faiths, is being steadily cast aside, and nowhere is this clearer than in the realm of religious belief. There is no quick or simple solution: the problem is too vast and too many-sided. Old in essence, it is here new in form, and it has the ruthlessness of new things.
The government will continue to use whatever means are available to support every effort to assert the principles of religious and political liberty and to restore their practice.

Mr. Speaker, on the order for
motions, and as arranged yesterday by the house, by unanimous consent, I ask now that consideration be given to the proposal I made yesterday calling for evening sittings from 7.30 to 10.30 during the period of the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne.
Perhaps to keep the record clear I should point out that after I offered my amendment yesterday to the motion of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) made what I regarded as a reasonable request, namely, that the amendment stand over until today. A few minutes later, on a question of privilege, I pointed out that it was not possible to permit the amendment to stand over without forcing the holding over of the main motion, thus preventing debate yesterday on the address. With that in mind I said this, as reported at page 720 of Hansard:
If the house will give its undertaking that we shall consider the matter tomorrow as a substantive motion, I am willing to withdraw the amendment. We can hardly let both the motion and the amendment stand over, because that would prevent the house from going on with the address today. If the house will give that assurance, I shall be glad to let this matter stand for consideration and decision by the house on a free vote at three o'clock tomorrow afternoon.
Not only was that offer made as a proper gesture, both to the leader of the opposition and to the Prime Minister, but the silence of the house at that point gave unanimous consent to the procedure suggested. Therefore I ask for consideration of that matter in the form of a substantive motion, moved by
House of Commons
myself and seconded by the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Nicholson), as follows:
That, except on Wednesdays, Mr. Speaker shall leave the chair at six o'clock p.m. until seven-thirty, and shall adjourn the house at ten-thirty p.m., without question put, until consideration of the speech from the throne is disposed of.
That wording is precisely the wording I gave yesterday, with one exception. Where the words "said speech" appeared yesterday, I have put in the words "speech from the throne".

speechtext:
As I was saying, many efforts have been made by members on all sides of the house to bring about some reform with respect to the time of house sittings. I think there is general agreement that some reform is desirable and that a decision in the matter must be made.
On June 25, 1947, I made a suggestion which I think had the support of many hon. members in all parts of the house. My suggestion was that we should sit continuously from one o'clock in the afternoon until seven o'clock at night. That suggestion was thrown out toward the end of the session so that we could deal with it and with other related problems at the next session. I think some twenty-seven different suggestions were made about changing the procedure and rules of the house.
As Your Honour knows, last year we set up a small but informal committee in an effort to iron out some of the difficulties which were bothering hon. members and which should be ironed out if there was to be unanimity as to the method of carrying on the business of the house. While some of us at that time were not in agreement with the original suggestion of seven to ten o'clock instead of eight to eleven, the view seemed to prevail that if we could not get something better, we might take that suggestion as it was.
Now the suggestion of the motion before us is seven-thirty to ten-thirty.
I am still of the opinion that this house should appoint a small committee, not to deal with all the ramifications of rules and house procedure, because again the discussions would go on until the end of the session, but to deal only with this question of house sittings. I hope that that will meet with the approval of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. It should not take more than a day or two. Let us do this in the proper way. The committee could then come back

to the House of Commons with something which would meet with general approval.
Certainly the present hours are too long. Hon. members cannot be expected to sit here year in and year out until eleven o'clock at night, when they start their work at nine in the morning. I think we would be regarded by the public as a sensible assembly if we changed the hours so that they would be more humane and tolerable to the average member. The committee could be set up at once, and perhaps before the end of this week we could arrive at some decision. It may be a decision for seven-thirty to ten-thirty, but I am not so sure that those hours meet with general approval. I suggest the immediate appointment of such a committee.

It is
obvious that there are various ideas as to what should be done about the hours of sitting of the house. I believe a suggestion was made last session by our own group that the house sit from two until six in the afternoon, and from eight until ten in the evening. That would not reduce the number of hours of sitting, and we could get through the same amount of work as we do now. We are not pressing that at this time, I am merely citing it to illustrate what I said to begin with, that various suggestions have been made, and [DOT] it seems to me they ought to be considered by a committee. I hope that the member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) will support the idea of having a small committee of the house set up to bring in a recommendation which would resolve the various suggestions into one that will be acceptable to the members of the house.

maintopic: MOTION TO CHANGE HOURS OF EVENING SITTINGS TO 7.30-10.30 DURING DEBATE ON ADDRESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I find that everybody is consulting his own convenience. While I am always ready to meet the convenience of others, it may be well for each of us to consider the propriety of engaging the House of Commons in a trial of this kind. The lives of most of us are fixed. We have habits, we have engagements, and vve have appointments. To undo them for the purpose of ascertaining what effect it will have upon our digestive organs to rush through a meal, which is generally late, for the next ten days, seems to me, with great respect, out of keeping with the dignity of the house, and with the practice of this deliberative assembly. If it is thought desirable to amend the rules, let us name a committee for that purpose, and let us amend them in an orderly and accepted way.
It seems to me we are asked to adopt a method of reaching a conclusion which is devoid of the precision and finality that should be characteristic of decisions of a body of this kind. I suggest that we do not depart from parliamentary practice. For a long time members have felt that the hours of sitting are long, but the sessions are long, too. I, for one, certainly do not wish to vote for a prolongation of the session. If curtailment of the hours brings about prolongation of the session, I do not think many members will 28087-49
House of Commons
support such a suggestion. We are asked to make an experiment to determine whether or not we should meet in the evening at half past seven instead of eight. Most of us work in our rooms until the dinner hour, seven o'clock; then we dine and come back here at eight. I am totally against a change in the order of our lives for two or three weeks. I believe that if a change is to be made it should be made after discussion, and after the pleasure of the majority has been ascertained by a committee.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: INSTALLATION OF SLIDE DECTECTOR FENCES
speechtext: I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Transport. Can the minister say what progress has been made in the installation of slide detector fences and other safety devices on the Canadian National railway lines in British Columbia, and what are the plans for future installations?

subtopic: INSTALLATION OF SLIDE DECTECTOR FENCES
speechtext:
The Canadian National Railways are installing at the present time block signals west of Kamloops, in conjunction with which they are to install three different types of slide detector fences for test purposes.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, to continue my saga of the Canadian portion of the Columbia river basin, may I point out that international problems respecting waters used within the Columbia river basin are subject to the provisions of two treaties signed between the governments of the United States, and of Great Britain on behalf of Canada. These are dated 1846 and 1909. The treaty of Washington of 1846 established the international boundary between Canada and the United States west of the Rocky mountains. Article II contains a provision with respect to navigation of the main stream of the Columbia river below the boundary of British Columbia.
I had intended to deal with certain aspects of article II of the Washington treaty, but as my time is limited I shall have to leave that for another occasion. Article IX of the boundary waters treaty of 1909 provides for the founding of the international joint commission, to be composed of Canadian and American representatives. That treaty was signed, and the commission came into being under the sponsorship of the late Theodore Roosevelt, who was then President of the 
United States, and under the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier, who was then Prime Minister of Canada.
I believe most hon. members recognize the fact that the international joint commission is a venture that has borne good fruit, and has stood as a lesson to the world in common sense and good will between nations. The international joint commission established its procedure on February 2, 1912. As a result of that it is now composed of three Canadians and three Americans, with a chairman acting for each section. The respective chairmen take the chair when the commission sits in the United States or in Canada.
The Canadian members at the present time are the Hon. Allison Glen and the Hon. George Spence. There is at present one vacancy. The commission has conducted many investigations and I have read with great interest many of its findings. I attended several of its hearings and am much impressed with the work it has done.
In 1941 the United States authorities applied for approval of certain levels of water that were going to be occasioned by the building of the Grand Coulee dam. That was after the dam was built, and I intend to have something more to say about that on a later occasion. The government of the United States and the government of Canada in 1944 agreed upon a reference to the commission with regard to the Columbia river. The Prime Minister of this country tabled that reference in this house on March 9, 1944. I should like to quote the first paragraph of the reference because it deals in brief with the instructions to the commission with respect to the Columbia basin investigation. That paragraph reads:
In order to determine whether a greater use than is now being made of the waters of the Columbia river system would be feasible and advantageous, the governments of the United States and Canada have agreed to refer the matter to the International joint commission for investigation and' report pursuant to article IX of the convention concerning boundary waters between the United States and Canada, signed January 11, 1909.
Later the same day the Prime Minister made a statement concerning this reference to the commission, which was a most important reference in so far as the people of the southeastern interior of British Columbia are concerned. The Prime Minister said:
The report of the international joint commission will not be binding on the governments concerned, but it is likely that the investigations of the commission will result in suggestions and recommendations which will be carried into effect by joint action of the two governments.
Pursuant to that reference the international Columbia river engineering board was appointed, composed of four members, two
77S

of whom represent Canada. The Canadian members are V. Meek, controller dominion water and power bureau, and F. G. Good-speed, assistant chief engineer, public works of Canada. In addition to this board, the Columbia river engineering and the Okanagan engineering committees were appointed, the Canadian members being C. E. Webb, chief engineer, dominion water power bureau, Vancouver, and M. K. Morton, district engineer of public works, Vancouver.
Immediately after the reference was tabled a full scale investigation was ordered and is now proceeding. This includes aerial photography, geodetic surveys, topographical mapping, bathymetric surveys, reconnaissance surveys, geological and damsite investigations, hydrological studies, climatology, soil surveys, survey of forest resources, mineral resources, fisheries problems and recreational resources.
I understand that the estimated cost of this survey to Canada will be approximately $700,000. The entire investigation will disclose the water power resources which in that part of the country are not now being utilized because of a lack of effective control and agreement. After the investigation is completed it is hoped that public hearings will be held at various points throughout the area particularly concerned, so that the points of view of the people and of all interests can be heard. I may say for your information that public hearings were held in various parts of Canada prior to the actual commencement of the technical investigation in connection with the St. Lawrence waterway. Recently I read in both the United States and Canadian press of proposals which had been made in the United States with regard to the building of a crib dam on the Arrow lakes for the storage of water. We all know that these are only suggestions or proposals but many people in my constituency and in the adjoining constituency are confused because they think that something is going to develop immediately as a result of these suggestions. We all know that nothing will be done until the joint international commission has report-sd, and that anything done then will be the result of joint action between the United States and Canada. I have here a copy of the Congressional Record which contains a resolution presented to congress on January 24 by Senator Mitchell. In view of the fact that my time is running out I should like to place this resolution on Hansard for the information of the house.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

speechtext: Is that agreeable to the house?

speechtext:

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
It is from the Columbia basin commission on the United States side of the line and reads:
Resolved by the Columbia basin commission that it hereby requests the international joint commission to direct its international board of engineers to give priority to studies and report on the storage of water in Arrow lakes. British Columbia, so that the commission may decide the amount of storage it will approve there, and if such report be favourable, that the Bonneville power administration and the United States, and the proper governmental agency of British Columbia and Canada, then proceed to negotiate for an agreement or agreements for building a storage dam at the outlet of Arrow lakes to impound 5,000,000 to 7,000,000 acre-feet of water, whereby British Columbia will receive an estimated annual revenue of $2,500,000 to $3,500,000 and the power plants at Grand Coulee dam and Bonneville will be enabled to produce an additional 500,000 to 700,000 kilowatts of prime power during the winter months, so that said dam may be built at as early a date as feasible, possibly by the winter of 1951-1952; and be it further resolved, that the commission urge the state legislature, the members of congress from Washington, Oregon, Idaho, and Montana, the governors of said states, and the president of the United States, to join in the above request to the American members of the international joint commission and the premier of British Columbia and the Prime Minister of Canada to join in the above request to the Canadian members of the international joint commission in the hope that the threatened electrical catastrophe to the Pacific northwest during the next five years may be averted, and that, instead, both the United States and Canada may have increased development and prosperity and a stronger national defence.
This resolution indicates the interest taken by Americans in proposed developments in Canada.
I have three or four suggestions to make before concluding what I have to say today. My first suggestion is in connection with the vacancy that exists on the international joint commission. In view of the fact that some of the major decisions of that commission will concern the province of British Columbia and particularly the Columbia river basin within that province, I suggest that the present vacancy be filled by the appointment of some one resident in British Columbia who is conversant with the opportunities that are presented in the development of this basin.
My second suggestion is that consideration should be given by this government to the development of the water resources in the basin under public ownership in co-operation with the government of British Columbia. I am recommending the establishment of a Canadian Columbia river basin authority, and in support of that proposal I should like to quote from the minutes of a committee of congress which sat in 1933-34 to consider this question and which reported with respect to the United States portion of the Columbia river basin as follows:
We believe in private enterprise-in the expectancy of rewards for honest endeavour, labour, initiative and daring-in the things that have made
776	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Herridge
America great. But some things are too big for private enterprise, and the Columbia river is one of these.
I trust that this suggestion will receive serious consideration. A most favourable situation exists with regard to the public development of the main stem of the Columbia because there is little private interest investment to consider in connection with the development of the potential 2,900,000 horsepower.
Up to date all the proposals in connection with the development of water storage and power have come from the United States side of the line; nothing has happened so far as our government is concerned. The United States are leading us in this direction. I have in my hand the Christian Science Monitor for January 24,1949, which contains this headline:
Truman Orders Columbia Valley Authority Plans
That is in connection with the United States side of the line. Farmer organizations such as the Grange, trade unions and co-operative societies are all backing the establishment of a Columbia river authority, but on this side our government remains dormant. I should like to quote again from the Christian Science Monitor of February 14 which contains the following report:
It would be extremely dogmatic to assert that a river could not be developed except by a valley authority modeled after TVA. But it is irrefutable that, despite the long years of effort by our other resource development and construction agencies, and the millions of dollars of expenditures, the Tennessee is the only river that has been completely harnessed and controlled in the interests of the people.
I am quite sure, Mr. Speaker, that members of all parties in the house would support public ownership and public development of power in an area such as this, if they appreciated the success of T.V.A.
My third suggestion is that, after this investigation is completed, the question of the development of the Columbia river basin should be referred to the standing committee on mines, forests and waters to study and report on the use of power resources in the basin. A similar committee was established by congress to study and report to congress on the great possibilities in the United States portion of the Columbia river basin. The people of the Columbia river basin, which includes East Kootenay, West Kootenay, Yale, and a portion of the riding represented by the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton), are greatly concerned in the development of the basin. They are anxious to see the establishment of the pulp and paper industry. They are concerned about secondary industries; they are concerned about the development of power for irrigation in the Okanagan district.
As a result of the interest of the people of these areas, and their understanding of the


importance of the question, I have received a large number of letters suggesting that it is time for the people to hold a conference which will include representatives of all types of organizations. I suggest that farm organizations, co-operative organizations, trade unions, boards of trade, women's institutes, rod and gun clubs, municipal councils, irrigation associations, and tourist camp operators should hold a conference in the near future in order to co-ordinate their ideas, and in order to be in a position to present them effectively to the commission and to the government. I suggest that it would be wise for the co-operative organizations of the area to take the lead because they represent the larger number of people. The people do not want the policies for the development of this area determined by directors of companies who reside in Montreal and New York. They want them determined by the co-operation of the federal government, the provincial government, and the people of the area. In any development financiers and industrialists, naturally enough, must first consider profits; engineers must consider kilowatts, technical details, location and structures. It is the primary duty of the members of this house to be concerned about the welfare of the people as a whole, and to see that these developments are carried on for their greater benefit, and to their advantage.
My fourth suggestion, Mr. Speaker, is that the Columbia river basin is rich in history and rich in possibilities for the taking of an excellent documentary film by the national film board. I believe if democracy is to function satisfactorily people must be involved in the administration of their own affairs. I believe further that governments of all kinds should do more to inform the people about the development of the country. Dry official reports and scanty newspaper articles are not sufficient. In my opinion all educational authorities should co-operate to present the facts concerning Canada in such a form as to stimulate interest, understanding, and pride in national, provincial, regional and local developments. I think that the national film board could make a great contribution towards arousing the interest of the youth of our country by undertaking a documentary film covering the development of the Columbia river basin. I offer that as a positive suggestion towards offsetting the forces of fascism and communism about which many people in Canada are concerned at this time, because I do not believe those forces can be overcome by verbal blasts or merely talking about them. I believe they are going to be overcome by interesting the people, and particularly the young people of the country,

in the co-operative development of the resources of the nation by federal, provincial and municipal governments.
I have endeavoured in the time available to present to the house some information concerning the Canadian portion of the Columbia river basin, and I have endeavoured to advance certain suggestions. I trust that many members of the house, and the government, will give serious consideration to my proposals. In my opinion a solution cannot be found to our problems by merely emphasizing our rights, but I do believe that we can achieve great things in the development of this basin if all the interests concerned, federal, provincial, municipal, corporate, cooperative, and private, are willing to accept their full share of responsibility. What an opportunity the development of the Columbia river basin, almost unknown to the majority of the Canadian people, offers for the democratic meshing of all these interests.
The residents of the Columbia river basin do not intend to be silent spectators in the coming drama of development but understanding and active members of the cast playing their parts with purpose, and in harmony, to the benefit of all, and to the benefit of Canada.
Right Hon. J, G. Gardiner (Minister of Agriculture):	Mr. Speaker, it will be four
weeks tomorrow since the house opened, and it is almost four weeks since the address in reply to the speech from the throne was moved. I want to take your minus uack to that time, and express my appreciation of the addresses made by the mover and seconder on that occasion, and also express appreciation of the very effective manner in which the new leaders who have taken their places in the house presented their opinions on that occasion.
The discussion which is before us at the present moment is based upon the amendment to the amendment which was moved by the leader of the C.C.F. party (Mr. Coldwell). I wish to read that amendment in order to bring its context back to the memory of the members of the house. On page 95 of Hansard I find the following:
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, seconded by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) I move:
"That the following words be Inserted in the amendment between the word 'address' and the word 'we': We regret that Your Excellency's advisers have failed to make provisions for the orderly marketing of our natural products, and for their exchange for goods needed in Canada, and for the elimination of speculation in foodstuffs.
We regret further that Your Excellency's advisers have failed to make provision for national health insurance."
I do not intend to say anything this afternoon about the latter part of the amendment
The Address-Mr. Gardiner to the amendment, but I take for granted that the first part of the amendment to the amendment has to do with policies associated with the marketing of natural products, and in particular the products of the farm. For that reason it is my intention to deal with the subject for some little time in the hope that I can remove some of the misunderstandings that we appear to have with regard to our present position in relation to trade.
Six years of war have intervened between now and the time when a very important action took place which has come back into effect since the war, and which many of us appear to have forgotten. The trade of Great Britain during the century preceding the present one was built up under a policy of free trade. I do not think I am stating something which is not fully understood on all sides of the house when I say that policy was advocated by what came to be known as the leaders of liberalism in those islands. The policy of free trade was continued until 1932, and there are some reasons why it was changed at that time.
Before going on to speak of those changes, it is a matter of record that although Liberal leaders in Great Britain first advocated policies of free trade, those policies later were taken up by the leaders of the opposition party, known as the union party, and advocated as persistently and consistently by that party as by the Liberal party. But in the early twenties a group came into being in Britain who did not believe in those policies. As a result of the experiences Britain and other countries had undergone during the war through which the nations of the world had just passed, they thought a great deal more could be accomplished by controls, by agreements and by quotas than through free trade. They were able to press their arguments with such force that two elections were contested in Britain within a period of about eighteen months. One was held in late 1929 or early 1930 and the other in 1931, and after the second election the representation was such that it became necessary to form a coalition government composed of Conservatives, Labour members and Liberals. The Liberals who entered that government undertook in due course to forget the policies they had advocated for a hundred years, and agreed that for the time being some other action was required in order to build up the trade of Great Britain and balance her position as compared with that of other nations.
They did not take that action without considerable pressure, much of which came from Canada and Australia. As a matter of fact I believe four of the great dominions of the British commonwealth undertook to see to it
778

The Address-Mr. Gardiner that the policies of Great Britain were entirely changed so that we should have a very wide preference in the British market. Those who were pressing for this change made one or two appearances in Britain during the period I have mentioned, when those two elections were held; and after returning from the first visit the then Prime Minister of Canada, the late Right Hon. R. B. Bennett, impressed on this house the thought that there were no longer any free markets in the world. He went so far as to say that it was very difficult to find markets at all, and that it was becoming more and more difficult to trade even with one another and maintain our prosperity. As a matter of fact he said that "where there were markets thirty years before there were no markets now and that where there were markets even ten years before there were no markets now."
Not only was that said by the leader of the government of that day; it was taken up also by the then leader of the C.C.F. party, Mr. Woodsworth, who agreed with Mr. Bennett. In fact Mr. Woodsworth thought Mr. Bennett had not gone far enough, and said there were no markets to be found anywhere. Well, certain policies were built upon those ideas which prevailed not only in this country but also to some extent across the seas, and I have here the legislation passed by this house on that occasion, which by the way is still in existence. Before reading from it, however, I want to read just one sentence from an article which was prepared by Mr. Bennett, dated December 2, 1930, replying to a statement made by Mr. Thomas in Great Britain, who said the policy being advocated by Canada and Australia and some other countries was humbug. Replying to that statement Mr. Bennett said:
I have declared on several occasions my willingness to favourably consider a quota system as a competitive method to that of tariffs for securing a preferred position for empire wheat in the United Kingdom.
Then in 1932 this house adopted legislation known as:
An Act respecting a certain trade agreement between His Majesty's government in Canada and His Majesty's government in the United Kingdom.
Article 1 in the schedule to that act reads: His Majesty's government in the United Kingdom undertake that orders shall be made in accordance with the provisions of section 4 of the Import Duties Act, 1932, which will ensure the continuance after the 15th November, 1932, of entry free of duty into the United Kingdom of goods consigned from any part of the British empire and grown, produced or manufactured in Canada which by virtue of that act are now free of duty subject, however, to the reservations set forth in schedule A appended hereto.
Schedule A provides:
As regards eggs, poultry, butter, cheese and other milk products, free entry for Canadian produce will
(Mr. Gardiner.]
be continued for three years certain. His Majesty's government in the United Kingdom, however, reserve to themselves the right, after the expiration of three years, if they consider it necessary in the interests of the United Kingdom producer to do so, to review the basis of preference so far as relates to the articles above enumerated and, after notifying His Majesty's government in Canada either to impose a preferential duty on Canadian produce whilst maintaining preferential margins, or-
This is the important part.
-in consultation with the Canadian government to bring such produce within any system which may be put into operation for the quantitative regulation of supplies from all sources in the United Kingdom market.
In that regard I want to call attention to the fact that in the first place the government of Canada insisted on having the free market in Great Britain for food products and some other items brought to an end, and then insisted on certain preferences for our own products in that market. In return for obtaining consideration in that market they agreed that it was quite right and proper for the British government to quota the imports coming to that market from any country in the world, including the countries of the commonwealth.
Let us examine for a moment what that meant. My first experience with that provision was in 1936. When I came to Ottawa as Minister of Agriculture I thought my main task in a federal government would be to promote the marketing of farm products, at the same time promoting their production in order that we might take advantage of the greatest possible share of the markets of the world that were available to us at that time.
I went to Britain in 1936 as part of the delegation that was going to deal with the provisions in that act. At the time when the British government was empowered by the act of 1932 to substitute quotas for tariffs as suggested by the late Mr. Bennett in 1930 and to apply them to the different countries which supplied their food, they took as the basis the quantity which we had sent into that market in 1935. They said that what Poland sent in 1935 should be the basis of consideration for that country; that what Denmark had sent in 1935 should be the basis of consideration in so far as that country was concerned; and that what Canada had sent in 1935 should likewise be the basis upon which our quantities were to be established.
If the operation had taken place exactly as planned, it would have resulted in our taking certain quantities in connection with bacon. The quantity which was discussed at great length was 160 million pounds, that being the quantity they understood we could produce because of what we produced in the preceding year. Then they said, "Why, you only sent over between six and seven thousand head

of cattle in the preceding year." When we spoke of a number approximating 60,000 head, we were unable to get them to write that figure into the quota.
The same condition existed in connection with our cheese. The quantity of cheese we had been sending over was very much less than we had sent over around the beginning of the century. We had hopes of increasing our cheese production. When we went to Britain to set down the quota in connection with cheese, we were unable to obtain quantities greater than those I have been mentioning to the house. This took place in 1936. Finally, we did succeed in having the British government give us an undertaking they would not check us further until we reached 280 million pounds of bacon; that they would not check us further until we got up to approximately 60,000 head of cattle, nor would they check us further with regard to our cheese production until we had reached 60 million pounds. The British government insisted, however, upon a very definite understanding that this food would be forthcoming. It was said that since they had given away opportunities of obtaining their food in a free market at the cheapest possible price, and since Britain had only 7 per cent of her population engaged in farming, the British government must be in the position of being assured of the quantities of food that would be forthcoming from the different countries of the world. We, being a federation, were unable to give that assurance.
As a new country, we offered this argument: We said that was all very well for some of the old world countries whose farm lands were fully occupied and who were producing to the limit. We said a new country such as Canada must have an opportunity of expanding, that tying us down to quotas of that sort would not give us that opportunity. In the years between that year and the war, we were successful in increasing our production considerably and thus placing much greater quantities of meat and dairy products upon the British market than in 1935. We had almost reached a point in that connection when further checks might have been made had war not broken out, but war came.
When the war came we transferred over from a policy of quotas established by agreement from year to year between governments to a policy of entering into a bilateral agreement to deliver to Britain certain quantities of food. I submit to this house, Mr. Speaker, there is not very much difference in principle between the two. There is not very much difference between being required to go to London every year and work out the amount of our quota, and sitting down from year to

The Address-Mr. Gardiner year and making a bilateral agreement such as we made during the war years.
I cite these facts, Mr. Speaker, in order to place in the minds of the members of this house the fact that some people who are very critical today of quotas, and very critical of bilateral contracts, were responsible for the creation of the conditions under which we have been working from 1932 to the present. In 1940, the first year of the war, this question came up when we were in Britain. I was there representing the agricultural people of this country and insisting that we had already produced over 300 million pounds of bacon in surplus in one year. I felt we could deliver to Britain over 400 million pounds of bacon in a year. I was told by the British government we had to accept one of two things: Either we could sell Britain 380 million pounds of bacon at the same price as we obtained the year before or we could sell that country 445 million pounds of bacon for the same amount of money; in other words, at a lower- price per unit. In order to keep our product in the market we sold it at the lower price which reauired a reduction in the price of bacon going to Britain, as I remember it, of approximately 11 shillings as compared with the price obtained the preceding year.
There is another fact I think we ought to remember at this time in connection with this matter. While our price was lower for the second year, our price for the preceding year had been higher than the United States price for hogs by from three to five cents a pound. I, as well as others, considered the British were quite justified in coming back the second year and requesting the product from Canada at a lower price in view of the fact that the cost of feed had gone down very materially because we had no market for our grain at that time. This lack of markets for grain was caused by the war.
To come back to the point I was making, the question came up as to whether we would prefer a better price for our bacon than was being offered or whether we would prefer to have a long-time agreement which would carry on for some years after the war. I suggested that, if anyone was prepared to discuss that question with us, we were prepared to discuss it. The discussion stopped right there. The next day we were told that the 1932 agreements and the quotas arranged in 1936-37-those quotas applied to the European countries and the commonwealth countries-would come back into force after the war. We would have to be prepared and the other countries would have to be prepared to meet a situation which would be created by the fact we had changed our policies in relation to trade, not only throughout the

Someone may say, but you have had a Liberal government since 1935 and you have not done away with that legislation. The question is obvious and the answer is just as obvious. There is not a free market in Britain as there was prior to 1932. There is not any free market because a protective market was forced upon the people of that country to a degree, or they were argued into it by their own leaders both in the economic field and in politics. Those new leaders convinced them of the effectiveness of new theories. Since that time, as every hon. member knows, the old Liberal idea of basing your prosperity upon trade has not held the same place in Great Britain or anywhere else that it held prior to the making of the 1932 agreements. If there have been any difficulties which have arisen as a result of the change, these difficulties no doubt have been brought about by the fact that there has been a change from free trade to preferences. The benefits of free trade cannot be re-established except by the British.
May I point out just for a moment what that means to us now? When we met to discuss the possible marketing of farm products in Great Britain from the time the turn came in the war in 1943 and 1944 down to the end, on every occasion, no matter what government was in power in Britain, the fact that was emphasized was that we were getting back nearer and nearer to the position where it would be necessary for us to come under these old arrangements which had been made previously, and therefore we had better start to govern ourselves accordingly. We did govern ourselves accordingly. We took 10,000,000 acres of land out of wheat production in this country in the early part of the war. We put that land into the production of livestock and livestock products. In the last two years of the war, and in the year immediately following the war, we put the greater part of those 10,000,000 acres back into wheat and we took the grain for human consumption rather than for the production of livestock. Therefore, we have changed over twice since the beginning of the war; first from the production of wheat into the production of livestock, and then back from the production of livestock into the production of wheat.
There are one or two questions which have been discussed in this debate, one by the new member from Nova Scotia. He comes from a constituency which is more concerned about it than any other constituency in Canada with

So far as I am concerned, personally, I would support anything in the house that would be the means of bringing down the cost of living, or of seeing that the people who are suffering from the high cost of living would have some relief. But before supporting any such thing I would want to be at least reasonably sure that the remedy suggested is a sound one.
The C.C.F. have made no effort in the house, either in this or in any other debate during the three years I have been here, to show anything to justify their contention that we should roll back the prices to the 1946 level. What would happen? The very day we rolled back the prices to the 1946 level we would find that merchants, large and small, in this country would have terrific stocks of goods on their shelves. Those stocks would be on hand, right from the manufacturers, through the wholesalers and jobbers and down to the retailers. Surely no government, C.C.F. or any other kind-if there ever was a C.C.F. government in Canada-could say that today we are going to tell a man who has on his shelves goods worth $10,000 that tomorrow those same goods would be worth only $5,000 because we are rolling back the prices to the 1946 level, and since that time the price has gone up twice as high.
If the government took that action, without making compensation to the manufacturers, merchants and others, it would certainly ruin all the small merchants and would likely ruin most of the big ones. If the government did not say, "You have to do it without compensation", and were prepared to give compensation, then I suggest no government this country has ever known could ever finance such a colossal scheme as would be involved in giving compensation to merchants, manufacturers and wholesalers for the goods they might have on their shelves. Until that can be explained to us, I will suggest that the Canadian economy cannot stand the process which is involved in the slogan of rolling back the prices to 1946. It would cost a great many millions of dollars, and certainly much more than our economy could stand.

How could we roll back the prices to the 1946 level when our economy is so tightly tied to that of the United States? Are we going to be able to reduce the standard of living in Canada below that of the United States? I suggest our people would not stand for that for one moment. In fact, they took with only the barest of good will-if one could call it good will-the austerity program already in force in Canada today, without any further differentiation between our standard of living and that of people in the United States.
I say this, too, that if the government were to begin to control prices, or to put price controls on again and make them retroactive, or if they were put on today without being made retroactive, it would kill the initiative to produce, and we would have less goods than we ever had. That was the story when controls were on, of necessity, during the war. It meant that we had less and less goods. And, what is more, we had goods of poorer quality as time went on.
If we rolled back the prices to the 1946 level we would create in this country a wave of blackmarketing which would mean that those whom hon. members to my left, the C.C.F., dislike so much, the people with wealth, could go on the black market and get what they wanted, while those of us who are not so fortunate as to have such a good supply of this world's goods would have to take what we could get.

I said it quite clearly. My charge is that apparently the government is allowing known supporters of nazism to enter and stay in Canada. I realize that there are those who will immediately cry out that in saying that I am taking the part of the communists. I refuse to keep quiet because words of mine may be deliberately misconstrued as those of a communist sympathizer. Anyone who attempts to place such a misconstruction on them is either a knave or a fool, and in all probability both. I, together with other members of my party, have opposed communists long before some members of this house even knew that they existed. The pity is that communists use the same words as do the staunchest believers in democracy, but they do so for their own ends. The pity of it is that communists fasten on to obvious wrongs and social injustices, not with a determination to correct those wrongs, but for their own purposes.
Perhaps I may be permitted to quote from a speech made by Mr. Justice Douglas of the United States Supreme Court last Friday in Los Angeles. Part of what he said is as follows:
We must restore integrity to our own political tactics by putting an end to the shameful practice of branding as a communist everyone who espouses a liberal reform or promotes a program for the underprivileged.
Of course, it may be said that the sources of my information are communist-inspired. I shall give them to the house. The sources of my information are newspaper reports,

and certain discussions I have had with those who wrote those reports. The newspapers concerned are the Montreal Herald-I doubt if it is under the domination of communists- the Montreal Standard and the Vancouver Sun. These are all good examples of capitalist journals in this country. I have another authority, and an even better one. My authority is Colonel Romans Petit, who is president of the national federation of maquis. A word about the maquis might be in order. The maquis are men who gave back to France her soul during the war. They are the men who gave back to France her honour after the betrayal of Vichy. They are the men who died, not only to free France from nazi persecution, but also to enable us to live in Canada as free men and women. The men of the maquis are heroes whose names will be remembered wherever there are free men. Colonel Romans Petit has the distinction and the honour not only of being a member of the Distinguished Service Order but also of being president of the national federation of maquis, a commander of the legion of honour, and a companion of the liberation. He wrote to us in response to a communication which was sent to him by my leader, the member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), after we had discussed the matter. We asked for information about Montel, Boussat, Hue and Labedan. This is the answer which we received; it has been translated. It is sent from Paris, and the date is February 16, 1949. It reads:
Replying to your letter of the 11th instant which I did not receive until today, owing to a mistake in the address, I hasten to advise you that I immediately got in touch with various persons capable of supplying you with the information you seek. With more particular reference to Doctor Montel, who was chief of the militia in Haute Savoie. I am asking one of my friends, well placed by reason of his position, to provide you with all exact documents, to communicate to you directly the main points of the charges laid against Montel.
I will add that personally in my capacity as leader of the maquis in Haute Savoie I suffered from the anti-national activity of this Frenchman, and we are happy to know that there are to be found in that great friendly country that is Canada men such as you to defend French prestige, and consequently the laws of honour.
The Be-nonvilles and fellow travellers hampered all our efforts in our struggle to save the country, and for that reason we deem them unworthy of your hospitality.
Then there are these brief dossiers:
Jules Labedan, bom 1/6/1913 at Gimont (Gers), domiciled at St. Gaudens, was sentenced to death at Toulouse 10/2/45 for treason.
Andre Boussat, born 20/10/1906 at Belves (Lot et Garonne), domiciled at Villeneuve sur Lot (Physician), was the subject of a warrant for arrest issued the 12/2/45 by the Court of Justice of Agen. He was member of militia No. G 44 2650.
Jean Louis Hue, commissioner of woods and forests, militiaman, was the subject of a warrant for arrest issued in Toulouse.
The Address-Mr. A. Stewart
Then I found today that another fish had come into the net. I asked the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. MacKinnon) if he knew whether or not Michel Lucien Seigneur was in Canada, and the answer was: "Yes, he is here." The information I have on Seigneur is as follows:
Michel Lucien Seigneur, bom 22/1/1907 in the Somme, physician, ex-inspector of the Waffen SS at Limoges-
That is, the blackshirts.
-deputy departmental chief of the militia at Poitiers, sentenced to death by the court of justice of Poitiers.	.
Then Colonel Romans Petit goes on:
We know that in Canada a certain opinion looks upon all resisters as communists, whereas I set store by my personal documentation; since I was in command of three very important departments, l'Ain, le Haut Jura and la Haute Savoie, there were only 15 per cent in our ranks. Personally, I was the object of very sharp attacks on the part of communists, after the liberation. It suffices to state that our testimony is influenced by no political consideration. We take our stand not merely from the viewpoint of French interests but also from the viewpoint of humanity. We cannot forget that the militiamen resorted to inhuman means towards all our people who fell into their hands.
We believe that you are in possession of a few depositions with reference to Bernonville. On behalf of all our resister comrades, I thank you, Mr. Member. and assure you of our deep consideration.
That is signed by Colonel Romans Petit, D.S.O., president of the national federation of maquis, commander of the legion of honour, companion of the liberation. There is one part which I think I might repeat and paraphrase. It is:
We take our stand not merely from the viewpoint of Canadian interests, but also from the viewpoint of humanity.
I repeat that I oppose with equal vehemence the entry of fascists and communists into Canada, but since only fascist collaborators appear to be coming here I shall devote myself to them. Yesterday I listened with some interest to the address of the leader of the official opposition (Mr. Drew). He spent much of his time dealing with communism, and the menace and the perils of communism. I had hoped that he might have had time to spare a word about the menace and perils of fascism, but apparently not. I assume that he is aware of what has happened. I know that the member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) has taken an interest in this matter, and I would have thought that perhaps he had discussed it with his chief. I do not know whether he has or not, but in any event I know that the leader of the opposition has been questioned in press conferences as to his attitude concerning de Bernonville, and perhaps others, and his answer, to the best of my belief, has been "No comment". "No comment" is not good enough comment

The Address-Mr. A. Stewart from one who is the head of a party which has pretensions to being a national party.
I ask the hon. gentleman to make his stand amply clear before this debate is finished. I said earlier that avowed fascists were entering Canada. There was a case which came to my attention, that of one Karol Murin, who apparently came here last September. Recently he has been in Winnipeg, and while there he permitted himself to be interviewed by reporters. He bragged of the fact that he had been the secretary of Dr. Tiso. I shall remind the house who Dr. Tiso was. Dr. Tiso was the puppet dictator appointed by Hitler in Czechoslovakia who was eventually hanged for his crimes by the Benes government.
This man told the reporters that under Hitler Slovakia had had six years of independence from 1939 to 1945. I think that is a man whom the minister could well afford to investigate a little further. Now on February 8, 1949, I asked a question of the minister as to where Count Jacques de Ber-nonville was. He told me, and I asked a supplementary question which was:
Is the minister aware that this man is a traitor, and that he betrayed allied soldiers to the gestapo?
There was no answer. No answer was necessary, because in his answer to my original question the minister gave me all I wanted to know, and in this case I assumed silence meant assent. The next day on a question of privilege the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay (Mr. Dorion) rose and stated that he was one of two counsel who had been appointed to act on behalf of de Bernonville; and he went on to say:
... I strongly resent the untrue and unfounded statement made yesterday by the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Stewart) . . .
As a matter of fact I had been very factual, as I shall prove later. The hon. member also went on to say he was convinced not only of de Bernonville's innocence but also of the assistance he had rendered our soldiers during the war. I think the most significant thing then was not the statement of the hon. gentleman but the applause coming from the Tory benches which greeted it. One of us is wrong. Either the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay is right or I am right, and I am prepared to leave it to the judgment of the house.
Briefly, Mr. Speaker, this is the background of de Bernonville; I shall give it in greater detail later. He was said to be instrumental in setting up in France a gestapo organization to rout out those who remained loyal to the allied cause during the German occupation. Many executions of those working for an allied victory resulted

from his efforts, according to information from France. During the North African campaign de Bernonville undertook to work for the German cause there. Again he established gestapo units to gather information among the French behind Rommel's lines. After the defeat of Rommel, de Bernonville escaped to France. This time the Germans made him military commandant of the Lyons area, a post that would go only to one of the most tried and true supporters of the nazi cause. His special task was to set up a counter-resistance police to combat the French maquis. In this he was concerned particularly with identifying British and other allied officers who dropped into France by parachute to aid the resistance movement. His work resulted in the death of many of these allied soldiers, it was said. This information came out during the Toulouse trial at which de Bernonville was convicted in absentia.
This man de Bernonville came to Canada in 1946, as did all those others I have mentioned. He was ordered deported, and the order was to take effect on October 6 or October 7. Then counsel appeared for de Bernonville, one Mr. Bernard Bourdon, K.C., who secured a writ of habeas corpus. The situation now, of course, is that de Bernonville is free; and I direct the attention of hon. members to a statement by the presiding judge, which I think is somewhat out of order:
The court ordered the count liberated immediately and said it was directing authorities at Ottawa to grant him asylum in Canada along with his family.
That is an amazing statement, and in it I think the judge went far beyond the bounds of propriety. However, to revert to Mr. Bourdon, according to the Montreal Standard of September 4 last he said:
de Bernonville is here as a political refugee, and there can be no deportation for a political crime.
What a pity Mr. Laval did not know that some years ago. Instead of going to Spain, from whence he was returned to France, he could have come to Canada where he might have obtained refuge as a political criminal. Later on Mr. Bourdon said:
Since I took over this case many important people have displayed an interest in it.
I am quite sure they have, but I should like to know who those important people are. How tremendously important and powerful they must be to be able to induce the government to upset the laws of Canada, to some extent, and allow in those who on many grounds are not eligible to enter this country. They must be tremendously important people. I remember last year when seven unhappy Jews were deported from this country
79S

because they had come in illegally. I spoke to the then minister about their case. I knew they had violated the law. I was afraid they might have to be deported, but I wanted to see if there were any grounds for clemency in their cases, in view of what they had suffered. The then minister said no; that if we should allow them to stay we would establish a precedent. That precedent had been established; I suppose the minister knew that all these fascists were here, but he deported those Jews who apparently had no very important friends.
On whose behalf was Mr. Bourdon acting? On behalf of de Bernonville, of course, but there is another character in the picture, a Mr. Jean Bonnel, of 4450 St. Denis street, Montreal. I am told that Mr. Bourdon was acting on his instructions. Now Mr. Bonnel is not a Canadian citizen but to the best of my knowledge is still a citizen of France. On October 16 of last year he was quoted in this way:
Bonnel says he is one of the main sources of aid to refugees from France accused of wartime collaboration.
And about the men with whom I am going to deal he said:
They are heroes of France. Instead of sending them to their deaths we should kiss their feet.
This seems a very odd citizen to have in our midst; but let me deal right now with this suggestion that if we returned these people we would be sending them to their deaths. The French ambassador has already disproved that in a press conference; and in addition Maurice Ribbet, batonniere of the Paris bar, while in Montreal for the meeting of the Canadian Bar Association, declared:
They can't shoot him if he returns home. Legally he is entitled to a new trial.
So they will not be shot if they return; they will be tried again, and tried in the courts of a country which is still a democratic nation. Then Bonnel goes on to say that he is one of the main sources of aid to collaborators. I wonder if the minister is aware of this. Is it possible, I wonder, that we have an underground railway into Canada by means of which these collaborators are being smuggled into this country? I know the department cannot possibly keep watch at every point on the border, but there are some of these people in this country, and they have been smuggled in. It is time the country knew how this is done. Then Bonnel said:
The four are not the only ones here. I could name you twenty living in Montreal. I have one working for me now. There was another here in this office this morning, a man under sentence of death with no passport at all. Nearly all the rest are here under false passports-naturally.
The Address-Mr. A. Stewart
Then he went on:
I will do everything to keep de Bernonville from being delivered to the present government of France, a government of cretins, assassins and bandits.
Now I think we can place this man Bonnel pretty accurately. Hon. members of this house will know how to judge those words, because there are very few of us who have not experienced the gracious hospitality of the representatives of France in Ottawa. If the minister has not done so already I hope he will make a point of investigating this man Bonnel to ascertain how he got here, what his record is and how, if what he says is true, he is bringing these people into Canada.
But I have another witness, though I am the first to admit that he is scarcely an asset to the democratic cause. I refer to Mayor Houde of Montreal, who said of de Bernonville:
Other members of his family, themselves under arrest in France, are day by day escaping to Canada to join him, one by one at the risk of their lives.
I would be the last to place any credence in what Mayor Houde says; nevertheless where there is smoke there may be some fire. This is another matter I think the minister might investigate. Mayor Houde made these remarks in a press release:
Twenty other refugees will be in the same tragic situation as the Count de Bernonville and will be deported also within the next few days. This iniquity should be unmasked. At the present time we are taking steps to see that this project is not executed.
I think we must admit that the steps taken have been, at least, adequate up to date. Then speaking of the deportation of de Bernonville, Mayor Houde said:
This crying injustice-we can call it this infamy- cannot pass in silence.
Just a few more words about Mayor Houde. At one time I think he was leader of the Conservative party in Quebec. I know that at page 2402 of Hansard for 1940, Mr. R. B. Hanson of the Conservative party placed on record a statement attributed to Mayor Houde in connection with national registration, as follows:
I do not myself believe that I am held to conform to the said law, and I have no intention of so doing, and I ask the population not to conform, knowing full well what I am doing presently and to what I expose myself.
It exposed him to a concentration camp. I can well understand how a man behind bars for hampering the war effort could feel such a close relationship for a nazi collaborationist. Obviously, birds of a feather are going to flock together.
