I have no time for either of them. Had the hon. member been in his place earlier, he would have heard that. I have heard further that the same Mayor Houde may be a Conservative candidate in the next general election. I should like to be enlightened about that. I wonder if it is for that reason the leader of the Conservative party has had nothing to say about this matter? After all, is the entry of known enemies to the democratic cause into Canada a matter of political strategy, of vote-getting?
If that is so, I can imagine how fascinated the father and mother of a boy who died overseas would be to know that he perhaps died at the hands of those who are getting succour in Canada. I can imagine how intrigued the widow would be who lost her husband overseas when she realized that these men perhaps had killed her husband and are now receiving sanctuary in Canada. It may be held that those who died are not important, but to allow fascist collaborators into this country is a betrayal of the memory of those who died fighting fascism.
I am going to deal in detail with de Bernon-ville. The first man whose statement I am going to quote is one Maurice Nedey, who was called one of the most remarkable figures of the resistance in a citation by General Charles de Gaulle, then provisional president of France, in August, 1945. Nedey received the Croix de Guerre 1939 avec Etoile de Vermeil for his wartime activities, as well as the Medaille de la Resistance Francaise and the British King's Medal "for courage in the cause of freedom".
The citation accompanying the Croix de Guerre award said:
Resisting from the first hour, he aided in the summer of 1943 the responsible Bureau des Operations Aeriens for the Saone et Loire.
He carried out numerous missions, both of a liaison nature and transporting arms. Constantly in the breach, he always endeavoured to reorganize parachuting services despite the gestapo's search for him. Arrested June 20, 1944, he was cruelly tortured, but did not deliver anything to the enemy on the organization to which he belonged.
He was one of the most remarkable figures of the resistance.
He received the King's Medal from the British government in November, 1946, from the hands of Alfred Duff-Cooper, British Ambassador to France, in a ceremony at Paris. The citation accompanying the British award said of Nedey:
(He) was the head of a leading resistance group in the Saone et Loire department of France. He organized several successful engagements against German patrols who tried to capture the material sent. Monsieur Nedey was arrested in July, 1944-
(Mr. Pouliot.l
I believe there is an error in the date, and that it should be June.
__and horribly tortured. He was deported . . . and
was recently repatriated to France.
I should like to read a statement made under oath and certified by X. Limal, an officer of the civil courts of France at Chalon-sur-Saone, dated October 25, 1948. This is the statement:
Nedey was arrested by Vichy police on June 20, 1944, during a secret mission from d'Allerey to Paris-l'Hopital. He was with M. Picard, liaison agent (Cote d'Or and Saone et Loire areas) for the Bureau des Operations Aeriens. The latter made good his escape.
Nedey was picked up near Chagny by the Group Mobile de la Reserve, but tried to make a break for it. He was recaptured some time later after a wild chase through vineyards-and after having swallowed two pieces of paper containing the messages which were the object of his mission.
May I interrupt my remarks here to say that if I do not have time during the forty minutes allotted to me to put all I know upon the record, I shall speak not only on the subamendment but on the amendment and, if necessary, on the main motion. Here is Nedey's statement:
After having been slapped and insulted, they brought me to the Hotel Moderne at Chalon-sur-Saone, which was headquarters of the Milice. On the night of my arrival the commander, de Bernon-ville, was absent. They tied my feet with electric wire, after having handcuffed me. and permitted me to lie down on the floor of the guard room. The adjutant ordered a strict surveillance.
I remembered then that a few days earlier members of the GRM (Groupe Mobile de la Reserve) had wanted to join the maquis. While the others slept, I asked my guard to take me to the washroom and I attempted to speak to him, telling him he had taken the wrong path; that everything was over for the Vichyites and that it would be better for him to help me to escape. I guaranteed he would have nothing to fear in accompanying me.
He told me he had two children and the reprisals would be terrible. I assured him real friends would care for them and they would want for nothing. He did not accept my proposition, but as I had confided in him I made him swear not to divulge our conversation to anyone.
The next morning, June 21. about eight o'clock the commander, de Bernonville. arrived and his subordinates informed him of my capture. My guard of the previous night gave a renort to the commander, divulging our conversation, on the grounds of attempted bribery of an official. They made me sign this document of my guilt. I could see my case was getting worse, but it was useless to deny the evidence.
After that, they brought me to a large room at the back of the hotel and de Bernonville sat down behind his desk which was in a corner. They cleared the tables and chairs and made me strip.
Present, in addition to de Bernonville were: the adjutant; a militiaman who had arrested me the day before; a man named Poitoux, who was killed a few days later by the maquis of St. Gengoux to atone for the tortures he had inflicted previously on many patriots; a militia lieutenant named Gelin, subsequently condemned to 20 years forced labour, and a GMR lieutenant named Delienne condemned to 10 years forced labour as a result of depositions

I made against them when I returned from Buchen-wald; and a civilian whose name is unknown to me.
De Bernonville, seated behind his desk, did not sully or tire himself to torture me; he merely gave the orders and led the course of interrogation. These orders were as follows: "Question him", "make him talk", "talk", "stop", "continue", "it's to your interest to talk and tell us all", "I am in a hurry and have no time to waste". All the staff I mentioned above rivalled each other in cruelty.
(Delienne and Gelin, according to another statement by Nedey, "saved their necks" at their subsequent trials "by explaining they had only obeyed de Bernonville's orders." The latter, they said, did not tolerate any laxity on their part in the fight against the maquisards.)
They spat on me, hit me with their fists, kicked me in the stomach. I warded off the blows as much as I could but one of them lashed me with a whip across the stomach and I thought I would vomit out my guts. I dropped to the floor time after time but they immediately made me get on my feet again by kicking me in the sides.
They stood in a circle and pushed me from one to the other. I began to realize I could not stand this for long. Then I got a tremendous blow which broke my lower jaw and I spat out bits of teeth broken by the shock.
De Bernonville demanded, in effect, the whereabouts of the maquis, the names of high-ranking officers, the location of arms depots, the passwords for various parachute districts, the dates of para-chutings, the location of the radio transmitter, the whereabouts of hidden British parachutists and the source of our orders.
I swore I knew nothing of these things, that the resistance organization was highly decentralized and that, to tell the truth, he had a mistaken idea of the organization of the resistance, and I could not tell him lies in order to satisfy him by swearing to things I knew nothing about.
If he had known I was in charge of the co-ordination of several maquis in our region, twelve parachuting fields, arms depots, a radio transmitter and two landing fields, I ask myself what fate would have been reserved for all the organization of our district.
Having been completely unsuccessful in the interrogation, he commanded my torturers to use electricity on me. They took a wire, which they spliced, attaching half to my handcuffs and pricking me with the other half, thus causing burns to my right arm and to the entire right side of my body and to my legs.
This process of torture was the most unbearable that I suffered during that unhappy year. It gave you the feeling of a knife turning in your breast, close to the heart. I curled up like a worm, crying out like a madman.
To keep me from moving, they passed a chair under my arm, blocking me against the wall. They gagged me to keep the noise from the neighbours. I was suffocating. For moments they would stop and prod me with questions, warning "Talk or we go on."
De Bernonville was impassive. I begged him to have pity and I recited prayers. I could stand no more and I could see my moral and physical forces diminishing. I was in utter turmoil.
In my innermost thoughts, I asked heaven for the strength not to denounce my comrades. Fortunately, I fixed this aim in mind; I didn't mind dying, provided it could be right away. I tried to stop breathing to suffocate myself, but nature was too strong. How I wanted to faint in order not to see or feel.
The adjutant took his revolver, loaded it and told me he would count to ten, promising to kill me if I didn't speak. But these threats were not carried out.
The Address-Mr. A. Stewart
These various tortures lasted all day with three-quarters of an hour of rest at noon and ended at seven o'clock at night. Then de Bernonville made me sign an admission which I had not even read I was so exhausted.
At night, when interrogation had been completed, de Bernonville told me I was a traitor and that it was a disgrace to work for England, that I had chosen my destiny badly and that, instead of having to face a firing squad, my fate would have been more glorious in working for the marshal, for France.
He told me that the June 6 landings on the shores of Normandy had been repulsed and, according to latest news, the enemy had been thrown back into the sea.
Amongst the enemy, of course, were a great number of Canadians.
He lectured me, saying the English, through their propaganda, had lost many young men like myself, and that if I were intelligent I would confide in him and he would do something for me.
I had the strength to reply that, since he called himself a true Frenchman, he should promise me at once not to turn me over to the Germans and I would undertake only to serve my penalty from the French. He acquiesced to my request, promising he would not deliver me to the boches. They took me then to prison, lodging me in a cell on the French side with French guards.
During the first night, I was sick many times. I was swollen, the skin of my thighs was in small cubes. I was unable to sit or lie down and I began to suffer terribly from my burns.
The guard of the French jail, M. Claustre, later said he had never seen a man in worse state enter the prison. He took it on his own responsibility the next morning to send for the prison doctor and to have me removed to hospital.
I could no longer open my mouth because of the fracture. My hands were completely dead and insensible. For a time it was even thought I would go mad.
On June 22, around six o'clock in the evening, I heard a guttural voice at the door of my cell and a militiaman turned me over to the gestapo, despite the promises of de Bernonville.

Mr. Speaker, it is fortunate for hon. members who support national unity that only the members of the C.C.F. party, fellow-travellers of communists in this country, approved the speech just made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Stewart).
Besides giving us the opportunity to hear panegyrics or interesting criticisms of the government, the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne enables

The Address-Mr. Gagnon most likely often reach an agreement if it came to applying the sanctions to others, but that they would reserve the right to avoid them individually. In short, a single vote, be it cast by England, the United States, the U.S.S.R., China or France, can bring about the collapse of the whole machinery. The only wars prevented, the only aggressions repressed would, in the last analysis, be those of small states. On the other hand, the great powers would retain complete freedom. As can be seen, the Dumbarton plan has some value only inasmuch as the co-operation between the great powers can continue after the war, just as it has been maintained during the hostilities. Then peace would be assured. But if the great powers no longer agree, we may expect the worst happenings, the worst catastrophes.
Such is, Mr. Speaker, the predicament in which we find ourselves. Our foreign policy 'which until now has been patterned on that of London now seems to copy that of Washington. Perhaps should I say it is dictated by Washington. From the way our leaders behave, you would think we were born to be forever in the tow of someone.
When, to appear as important as our powerful neighbour, neutrality is claimed to be impossible, is it not forgetting that history has proven this a fallacy? What of the examples, in the last war, of such countries as Ireland, Portugal, Spain and Switzerland? The august words from the sermon on the mount "Blessed are the peacemakers" should be carved on the entrance of all legislative buildings in the world.
We do not want any more wars, nor do we want to be buried again under taxes as we have been before and after the war of 1939. It is too great a burden for the poor, the lowly, the mass of the people. They are tired of handing over part of their pay check to these gentlemen in Ottawa. They are weary of the endless fuss and forms inflicted on them by dominion government civil servants.
The Department of National Revenue has behaved and still behaves revoltingly toward the taxpayers of the country. Worthy fathers are deprived of the very part of their earnings they require to educate their children, to supply them with medical care, to build a house and buy all the commodities essential to anyone's happiness. In my constituency, the salaries of some workers have been iniquitously garnisheed. Employers, merchants, small grocers are, if at all possible, stripped of their smallest profits while goods are squandered. The people are living in a reign of terror. They are wondering whether tomorrow National Revenue inspectors will not invade their homes to relieve them of the few dollars they have left.
I submit that when the state levies such heavy taxes on the small incomes and savings of its subjects, it is laying hands on something

that does not belong to it. The income tax act is anti-social, criminal both in origin and purpose. It is with such measures that unrest is created among the people, that elections are lost and that socialist and communist propaganda is fostered. To those responsible for Canada's destinies, I wish to say: Some day, you will have to account for your administration. Take care, for if ever our economic system is overthrown by a revolutionary movement on account of your accumulated mistakes, you will be among the first who will have to answer at the bar.
When taxes are too heavy, they have disastrous effects on savings. Now, as savings are absolutely necessary to make up the capital which fosters trade and industry, it follows that if they are discouraged, the original source of all undertakings is dangerously dried up. As His Holiness Pope Pius XII said to the members of the international congress of public finance:
For the sake of human conscience, do not destroy morals from the top. Refrain from legislation which, in spite of its brilliant technique, offends and hurts the people's appreciation of equity and inequity, or take small account of its vital strength, its rightful desire to reap the fruits of its own labour, its concern for domestic security, all of which considerations should come first and not last in the mind of the legislator.
The Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) was amazed the other day when those who disagree with him on centralization stated that the federal government is making the most of circumstances, and creates them if necessary in order to seize provincial rights as well as revenues. If it is prepared to forgo rent control, to leave to someone else a problem it has created but failed to solve, if the government is that careful not to encroach upon the powers given to the provinces by our constitution, why then, rather than announce in the speech from the throne the setting-up of a royal commission to look into the activities of certain bodies related to certain aspects of our national life, radio broadcasting for example, does it not withdraw from that field?
With the setting up of the Canadian Radio Broadcasting Commission in 1932, the central government entered the field of education, which was explicitly allotted to the provinces. Through the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, they monopolize the waves, they secure the air, the better to drown the private radio stations.
In the report of the special committee instituted to inquire into the setting up of a Canadian broadcasting system, it is said that

the evidence has confirmed the opinion of the committee as to "the great importance and advantages of an appropriate and well regulated broadcasting system for the whole of Canada as an instrument of education, guidance, religious and ordinary teaching, etc." And further on: "Our committee recommends moreover the establishment of a certain number of stations of 100 watts or less, operating on divided channels, located where it will be necessary for: (c) the needs of education." If the government are sincere when they protest that they are not centralists, then let them return to the provinces the rights of which they have deprived them. Let them refrain from violating, at every opportunity, the clauses of the British North America Act and let them mind what is exclusively their business.

In a talk he gave before the Montreal rotary club on February 8 last, the present Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) tackled the problem of mental hygiene with determination; he suited the action to the word.
The statistical picture he drew of the heavy toll which mental deficiency or nervous disturbances levy on mankind ought to make all our people think twice. If we add to this the incalculable risks resulting from background and heredity, we must admit that for those who are free from political worries and realize what a heavy responsibility rests upon them as well as upon our leaders, it becomes an imperative duty to solve this problem.
Here are some of the figures supplied by the Minister of National Health and Welfare in his talk before the Montreal rotary club on February 8.
In the course of a lifetime, one person out of ten suffers from emotional trouble of some sort; moreover, one out of ten needs hospitalization or psychiatric treatment.
The various degrees of mental illness range from mere emotional trouble to complete dis ruption of the intellectual faculty. Con-

The Address-Mr. P. Gauthier sidered from this angle, mental and nervous diseases produce more sick people than cancer, poliomyelitis and tuberculosis. There are in the hospitals giving treatment for these diseases just as many patients as there are patients being treated elsewhere for any other illness, except tuberculosis. We have had as many as 50,000 people suffering from mental or nervous diseases in the hospitals of this country. During the five years following 1930, the number of such cases increased in Canada by 26 per cent.
Was this due to the depression? I cannot say for I did not carry my investigation far enough to say so definitely, but in any event, this increase occurred during the depression. However, during the five years that followed, the increase was reduced by one half and, from 1940 to 1946, it came down to 9 per cent, which is 2 per cent more than the general increase in population. A rather dismal picture, as you can readily see.
In clinics and in dispensaries where the public is admitted physicians report that four out of ten patients suffer from emotional or nervous disturbances.
It must not be forgotten-and it is here that the problem becomes most acute-that along with the generally recognized forms of mental ailments, there are the related problems of juvenile delinquency, drug addiction, chronic alcoholism, pathological disregard of law, suicide and divorce. Anybody who has any knowledge of these problems at all will recognize that this list reveals a serious condition in the emotional syndrome and perversion of the social sense.

The younger brother told me however that one of his older brothers was still without a home, despite the fact that he had been slightly injured overseas. A pension of $12.50 had been awarded him. He was boarded six times within a year and a half, at the conclusion of which his pension had been reduced to $2.50.
That is the sort of thing these young men are talking about; and I say the minister must cure some of the evils before he can expect to get the response for which he is hoping in respect of enlistments in the permanent forces.
At the same time I was told that one of the brothers had served nearly five years in a heavy artillery unit of the army. The claim is now made that he is not pensionable, owing to the discovery by some medical doctors of what is alleged to be a pre-enlistment condition. This ex-soldier is faced with the necessity of having to fight for his rights to obtain some type of pension.
These are the things which the younger men, those who would be eligible for enlistment, are complaining about. They have learned a good deal from their older brothers who have had experience. Then, I am asked about the setting up of the committee on veterans affairs. These veterans cannot understand why the government does not recognize the many problems which should be considered at this time. I should hope the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Gregg) would give some opportunity for a general review of the many problems connected with veterans affairs.
Then finally, Mr. Speaker, we come to the question of housing. It was almost pathetic to hear what this young man had to say in that regard. He spoke of a soldier boy with one child who had tried to get one of the wartime houses.
I called upon what is now the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation at least a dozen times on behalf of a chap who is living in one room with one child up on the third story. I do not blame the local administrator, because he is just a chief clerk who is doing the best he can. He told me that he could not give that man a house unless he had at least two children. It seems too bad that a young man with only one child cannot be provided with one of these wartime houses when he was told overseas in most emphatic terms that the housing problem would be taken care of for him when he got home.
808	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Lockhart
In this particular case I told the young man to go down to the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to get one of the one hundred and two houses that had been built on what we call the Westchester avenue cut. He took my advice and made application for a house, but he could not get one because he is a pieceworker and was not considered to have employment of a permanent nature. These houses are rented at $42 per month, but before he could get one he would have to be engaged in the category of employment that would make him practically an annual asset. I could not believe it, but I checked and found that it was practically true.
I submit that the government is not doing its duty to the returned man. Aside from the inconsistencies that have developed in pension rights and the like, the first duty of the government is to provide them with homes.
Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation is developing something in the constituency of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) to which I strongly object. A couple of weeks ago I saw a development that has been started outside of Niagara Falls, at a point which seemed to me to be miles from civilization. I would say that about one hundred houses have been erected all cut from the one die; there is not a particle of difference in any one of them. They are small homes on forty-foot lots. Apparently Central Mortgage is still adhering to the forty-foot lot.
The roadways are made up of a few loads of stone scattered over the mud. I saw a mother with one child of two holding her hand and another baby in a go-cart having to take a most circuitous route in order to get to the main road. She had to walk three-quarters of a mile at least. I say that that kind of thing is not good enough for our returned men. I hope the Minister of Labour will check this up and I shall be glad to give him all the information I have.
It is time that something was done that would have a better influence for good among the men who fought for us during the past war. If the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) would listen to some of these stories-I am sure many hon. members have heard similar stories-he would understand why his enlistment program has not reached the point that many of us thought it would.
I come now to another matter which I should like to impress upon the government. The other day an hon. member referred to unemployment in Vancouver. Our socialist friends to the left were complaining bitterly about the many thousands of unemployed. There is one thing I should like to lay defi-


nitely on the doorstep of the government. I know just what transpired. During the war people were coaxed, and I say that advisedly, to leave small villages and rural areas to move into urban centres in order to produce munitions. Houses were built for them. In my own city some six or seven hundred so-called wartime houses were erected.
When the war ended those people refused to move back to the farm. The result is that we are short of butter, bacon and cheese and we hear the agitation for margarine. The wheel goes around and around. The government has fallen down in this matter. If it could induce people to move into the larger centres like Vancouver, Hamilton, Toronto and Montreal and provide them with housing, it is the government's responsibility when they have control of everything else to see that those people move back to the environment from which they came. That may be a broad statement to make, but the municipalities should not be imposed upon without some consideration and help.
It is not fair to try to coax masses of people into urban centres and then leave them there to be a direct responsibility of the municipalities. I strongly condemn the government for its failure in this respect. We are bringing in people with an agricultural turn of mind to go onto these vacant farms. There are many vacant houses out in the wide open spaces. Even in my own thickly populated area there are many houses available on the back concessions. These places are being occupied by displaced persons and other people who have been brought in.
I asked a question today about television, but I had a brush-off. That may be all right, as we are used to it, but I want to say a word more about this matter. Somebody has said that unemployment is growing. I am not so sure it is not, but I notice that the United States government is laying a cable to link fourteen major cities from New York to St. Louis in a television network. I read in this publication that there are more than 300 applications. As a matter of fact, it says that perhaps 400 are pending. There is a very interesting picture in one of the magazines. An enthusiastic purveyor of ice cream, soft drinks, sandwiches, candy, and so forth, has installed a television hook-up right in his place of business. The picture shows upwards of seventy-five children sitting in an orderly fashion drinking soft drinks, Coca-Cola, and drinks of that kind, others eating ice cream cones, and all apparently watching the television pictures that are being thrown on the screen. The man was interviewed as to why he did this, and he said that he was convinced that we have to do something to keep the children off the streets.

I suggest that, if the country to the south of us is going after television in a big way, it is time for the government to make some announcement and let the people know whether we are or are not interested in this most enticing development, perhaps one of the greatest that this country has ever seen. I am told that at the present time there are 16,000 receiving sets being made per week in the United States. I have talked to radio men in my own home city, and they say that they are cancelling orders for radios simply because they think the public are beginning to feel that television is just about to break. They do not want to buy machines that may become obsolete in a very short time.
I mention this matter to the government because it is a common topic among many people, and I say it is high time that the government paid a little more attention to it. I can assure the government that it is a very moot question in my own particular area because we are close to the border. There are many views that one might express, but I said at the outset that I was attempting to reflect in a small way some of the things that appear to be worrying people in my own constituency. My people say that while they put up with controls without much protest during the war, four years afterwards they find that there is a great army of snoopers, as my leader called them, and that is what a lot of them are. They feel that it is about time something was done to curtail that type of thing, and to reduce the cost of government, especially when we have floating around in the hands of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), as I said before, an odd billion or more which has been taken from the people unjustly. In attempting to show some reason why their circumstances are not just as they ought to be, I have pointed out that they are given the brush-off by controllers, by men in high places not responsible to parliament. I say it is high time that the government assumed their responsibility to a greater extent than they have.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset of my remarks I must confess that I intend to discuss a number of subjects in view of the latitude given to hon. members in this debate. I intend to discuss matters pertaining particularly to my own constituency and, as a matter of fact, to the people of Canada as a whole. The speech from the throne was disappointing in many ways, at least to me. One way in which it is disappointing is the fact that no mention was made of irrigation. Not one word was said about supplying water on our western plains.
I have spoken in every debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne
The Address-Mr. Wylie since I have been in the house, and I offer no apology for again devoting my time to a further discussion of the possibilities of irrigation for southeastern Alberta. The development or irrigation perhaps means more to the city of Medicine Hat than to any other community in Canada.
I must congratulate the mover of the address, the hon. member for Essex West (Mr. Brown). When he finished his speech I felt that I knew Essex West, and that I knew Windsor. Some members may think that it is bad taste to always discuss the problems of one's own constituency, but until those problems are solved I think that we are forced to do so. While I shall not attempt to duplicate what the hon. member for Essex West said, I shall certainly do the best I can to give the members of the house a few details about my constituency. Speaking of irrigation, I must mention at the outset that in my constituency we have some irrigation projects and we have areas which it is impossible to irrigate. First of all I want to mention the Taber area south and west of Medicine Hat. It is one of the best areas in western Canada, and the farmers specialize in the growing of sugar beets and many other field crops. A new factory is being built at Taber which will take care of the production in that district by 1950. They go in for diversified farming, raising stock and feeding them on the pulp from the sugar beets. In driving through the district surrounding Medicine Hat, and on west, one cannot help noticing the difference in the climate as soon as you get to an irrigation district. The air is entirely different; you think you are in a different climate.
Then we have the eastern irrigation district at Brooks, the largest in Canada, where they have 170,000 acres under irrigation. That is "where water works wonders." I think that is a wonderful slogan, and it certainly is true. They do not have a sugar beet factory in that area but go in for the raising of many other crops. Just to mention a few, they raise canning crops, field vegetables, root crops, vegetable seeds, tree and small fruits, field crops and many others. I might also mention that the Canadian championship for barley was won by Mr. Thomas E. Brown, who comes from Cassils. Many other records also could be mentioned coming from the eastern irrigation district, but I need not take time to do so. In passing, however, I think I should mention the pheasant shooting in that area. The Brooks area without a doubt is one of the finest pheasant-hunting districts in Canada. Sportsmen come all the way from eastern Canada to shoot pheasants there.
As you go further west you come to the western irrigation district at Strathmore,

The Address-Mr. Wylie which comes down to Cluny and Gleichen, another prosperous area through which it is a pleasure to drive. That was especially so last summer, when they had wonderful crops in that district, just showing what irrigation can do for a country. The rainfall seems to become more abundant as water is spread over the land and more trees are planted.
The residents of southern Alberta have been marking time for many years waiting for irrigation. We have two projects that affect Medicine Hat in particular; the St. Mary-Milk river project and the Bow river development project, which is more familiarly known as the Canada Land and Irrigation project. Before discussing irrigation further, I want to say that, after listening to the right hon. the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) this afternoon, it seems to me it should not be necessary for me to take up any time in this house discussing this subject. After all he told us about what the Liberals had done-

We are not just sure where
that is. The speech of the minister this afternoon would lead one to believe that all the farmers were satisfied and that no one had any complaints. That is not the case. In southeastern Alberta, where we need irrigation, the farmers have plenty on their minds. I want to refer for a moment to the Meek report, published back in 1942, which made this finding:
That Canada should construct at an early date the necessary irrigation works to protect by beneficial use its share of the St. Mary and Milk rivers.
I realize the government has made a start on a dam there, but it is a long way from completion and we in that area will not consider that project finished until we have water from that dam running through the city of Medicine Hat. The report goes on:
That there is tributary to the St. Mary and Milk rivers a larger area of good irrigable land than can be irrigated by the total water available from Canada's share of these rivers supplemented by waters of the Belly and Waterton rivers.


That upon the completion of the ultimate development a total of 345,000 acres would be available for post-war settlement and for the re-establishment of many farmers at present on submarginal lands.
How true that is. A short time ago I said that residents of that area have been marking time for many years waiting for the government to do something in the way of irrigation. Today we have many farmers who are ready and willing to settle on irrigated land. Then let me read another section of the report:
That with irrigation, soil and climatic conditions in southern Alberta are highly favourable for the production of livestock and for growing forage crops, sugar beets, com, and a wide variety of specialty crops.
That the stabilized agriculture and increased production resulting from further irrigation development in southern Alberta would provide for permanent home building, for a higher standard of living, and for improved social advantages and educational facilities.
I think we all realize that is the case. It must be remembered there is never adequate moisture to assure even a good grain crop in the dry areas of southeastern Alberta. The annual average precipitation in that area is 12-70 inches. The average rainfall for the two vital growing months of July and August is only 2-8 inches. Root crops require a great deal more moisture than grain. Further factual data is available to show that the land with which we are concerned is rich in protein-giving elements and capable of greater production if properly irrigated than the irrigated lands in many other parts of the west. I think that is a well-known fact.
In the years in which we have some rain, I could not say sufficient rain, we can grow crops. We can grow wheat in that area with less moisture than is needed in many parts of western Canada. I might add to that by saying that the wheat in that area is of better quality than in many parts of the west. In that area we also have from a minimum of ninety days to as high as one hundred and forty days wholly free from frost, and that is another matter which must be taken into consideration when planning for irrigation.

Perhaps he does, but when he goes out west I do not think he is so hot that he stops the frost. Irrigation would bring diversified agriculture, which is so essential to any community's prosperity. It would cushion the shock of any business recession which we hear so many people predicting is now on its way. It would reduce the cost of living by providing products now imported over long hauls. After listening to some of the discussions on freight rates, I think that

is a very important point. Many of these products could be produced right at home.
It would give stability by establishing new enterprises which were not so dependent on generally prosperous business conditions throughout the country. It is wasteful and shortsighted economics to allow these southeastern lands to remain undeveloped. It was Herbert Hoover who once said:
Every drop of water that runs to the sea without rendering a commercial return is a public waste.
I think that is a statement of which the Minister of Agriculture should take note, especially after the speech he made this afternoon. There are several good reasons why the government should give serious consideration to completing the Bow river extension with as little delay as possible.
The provincial government completed the agreement between the province and The Canada Land and Irrigation Company over various lands in the area affected. The main ditch has been completed over its entire course to Redcliff. A lot of people do not realize that fact when irrigation projects are oeing discussed. It will cost less to complete that project than to complete any other project in western Canada under consideration at the present time.
On motion of Mr. Wylie the debate was adjourned.

REFERENCE TO SPEECH OF MR. GARDINER ON FEBRUARY 22
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before you leave the chair, I wish to rise on a question of privilege. This afternoon I was quite unavoidably absent when the right hon. the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) spoke. I am told he gave a typically inaccurate account of certain events which transpired when his government was defeated at the polls in Saskatchewan in 1929. I understand he charged that I supported the entry into a coalition government of the Progressive and independent members of the legislature under the late Dr. Anderson.
Privilege-Mr. Coldwell
Not only did I not support it, but I opposed it vehemently and strenuously because I disagreed with the type of campaign conducted by Dr. Anderson and his friends. The Progressive party was disbanded when two of its elected representatives entered the government against my advice and that of the other members of the executive. I immediately assisted in the formation of labour and farmer groups which culminated in the C.C.F. party in 1932.
By one of those coincidences that sometimes occur, I received a letter last Wednesday from Dr. Hugh MacLean, a very respected citizen of Regina, now retired and living in Los Angeles, in which he reminds me of the true and quite different story. He speaks of a certain person, who shall be nameless. He says:
-the henchman who approached me when I wrote him (the present Minister of Agriculture) that he would have to retract his statement in which he denies that anyone had gone to you at his request after the election of 1929 and offered you a position in his government if you could prevail upon the progressives to support him. I insisted that his statement to the press would have to satisfy me and you, else I would tell the whole story.
The statement, admitting the facts was given to the press by the minister in the form of a letter. Somewhere, I have an original of that letter. The minister's statement this afternoon is absolutely incorrect for I was bitterly opposed to the Ku Klux Klan and its activities, as were many of my friends. As a matter of fact and record, my advice to the Progressive members was to remain independent and support all good legislation. They did not heed my advice.
May I ask the acting leader of the government what the order of business will be for tomorrow?
